h: A Bit of History With Your Sharks
p: Here's a fun fact to bring out in the queue: the building was designed by Eugenius Birch, the Victorian engineer behind Brighton's much-missed West Pier, and it opened its doors in 1872. That makes it a proper Victorian veteran, and when you walk under those arches it's easy to picture Victorian day-trippers in their Sunday best peering into the very same spaces. The tanks and the creatures have moved on a fair bit since then, but the bones of the place are pure seaside heritage.

Timing makes a big difference here. Brighton fills up fast on sunny weekends and bank holidays, and the aquarium gets busiest on wet afternoons, when everyone on the front has the same idea at once. Going first thing, or later in the day, usually means more elbow room at the glass and a better view of the bigger tanks. Booking online before you travel saves standing about on Madeira Drive too.

If you've got little ones, let them set the pace. Some kids will happily stare at one tank for ten minutes while others want to race to the sharks, and the route is easy enough to double back on if someone missed their favourite.

Once you're back out in the sea air, you've got loads of ways to round the day off. Brighton Palace Pier is right opposite, with its rides, arcades and doughnuts, while the British Airways i360 viewing tower further west gives you a bird's-eye view of the whole coastline. Fancy something grander? The Royal Pavilion, George IV's wildly over-the-top seaside palace, is only a short walk inland.
